title: When every cache misses at once
teaches: Thundering herds and stale sets, leases, invalidation from the database's log, and caches across regions

parts.title: Two and a half hours in September

blocks.text: On Thursday 23 September 2010 Facebook went down for about two and a half hours, its worst outage in four years. That evening Robert Johnson, who ran its software engineering, posted an account of what had happened, and it is short enough to retell in full.[^johnson]

Facebook kept some configuration values in its [[memcache|cache]] servers, copied from a cluster of databases. An automated system watched those cached values, and when a web server found one that looked invalid, it queried the database for the persistent copy and wrote that back into the cache. That day an engineer changed the persistent copy of one value, and the checker took the new value to be invalid. Every web server that read it saw an invalid value and set out to fix it, and every fix was a query to the same database cluster. Hundreds of thousands of queries a second arrived at a cluster built for far fewer.

The cluster slowed, then began returning errors. The fixing code read an error from the database as one more invalid value, so it deleted the cached key and tried again. Now the deletes guaranteed misses, the misses produced queries, and the queries produced errors. Reverting the bad value did not stop the outage, because the loop no longer needed the bad value to keep going. In the end the engineers had to stop all traffic to that database cluster, which meant turning the site off, and bring it back slowly.

Throughout, we will look for a [[feedback loop|busy]], a system response to overload or failure that generates more load. A cache is especially prone to feedback loops because it sits in front of a slower, more fragile storage system. The moment the cache fails to answer, the traffic it was absorbing goes straight to the database behind it. In this lesson, we examine how engineers handle cache misses, including hot keys that expire, stale values written by slow readers, and cache deletes that get lost.

Take one **hot key**, a key that is read far more than the rest, such as a celebrity's profile, a front-page story or a configuration value every page needs. Say 1,000 web servers read it 20,000 times a second between them. It is held in memcache in front of a database, used cache-aside as we saw in lesson 5: read the cache, and on a miss, query the database and set the result in the cache.

Consider the request rates. While the key is in the cache, the database receives zero queries for it. When the key expires or is deleted, the next reader misses and sends a query. If that query takes 50 ms, the key stays missing for those 50 ms, and in that time 20,000 × 0.05 = 1,000 more readers miss and each sends the same query. That burst of identical misses is a **thundering herd**. Sending 1,000 copies of one query wastes capacity, though if the database maintained its 50 ms latency under load, the extra traffic would end after 50 ms.

The database does not maintain its speed. As we saw in lesson 2, queueing latency grows without bound as a server nears 100% utilisation. Suppose the database can execute 100 concurrent queries at full speed, giving a throughput of 2,000 queries a second. Given more than 100 concurrent queries, it shares its CPU time evenly among them, so with 1,000 queries in flight each runs at a tenth of its normal speed, a scheduling model called **processor sharing**.[^ps] The herd generates 20,000 queries a second. The first query, whose completion will refill the cache and end the herd, now shares the database with hundreds and then thousands of duplicate queries, and every query slows down as more arrive. Higher database latency extends the cache miss window, and a longer miss window allows more duplicate queries to arrive. Make a guess before you run the simulation.

blocks.caption: A hot key expires. The database model shares its CPU time among concurrent queries, so a large herd increases the latency of the query that would refill the cache. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Guess, then turn leases on and play the two seconds through

blocks.text: At 2,000 reads a second the herd reaches 100 queries and the key is back in the cache in 50 ms. At 4,000 reads a second it reaches about 270 queries and takes 70 ms. At 10,000 reads a second it reaches several thousand queries and takes over 500 ms. At 20,000 reads a second the first query takes about 40 seconds to finish, and in that time the herd grows to hundreds of thousands of queries. The system tips from normal operation into overload across a tenfold increase in read throughput, and the threshold is the point where the rate of cache misses exceeds the database's maximum throughput.

Two common design choices make this overload worse. The first gives hot keys a short **time to live** (TTL) so they expire every few seconds to stay fresh, which triggers a new thundering herd on each expiry. The second retries failed queries automatically, which is the loop that took Facebook down in 2010. Once the database begins returning errors, every retry sends an additional query to a server that is already failing from overload.

In April 2013, at the NSDI conference in Lombard, Illinois, Rajesh Nishtala and his colleagues published "Scaling Memcache at Facebook", describing how they built memcache into a system serving billions of requests a second over trillions of cached items. One of the first problems they addressed was the thundering herd, which they solved using a **lease**.

In GFS, the master granted a lease to a chunk's primary (lesson 7), and in lesson 11 a consensus leader held one. A lease is a time-limited grant that permits a single node to perform an operation while other nodes wait. Facebook's lease applies the same mechanism to an individual cache key. When a client misses, the memcache server issues it a [[lease token|clock]], a 64-bit integer bound to that key. The token authorises the client to populate the key, and the client must present the token when writing the value to the cache.

The herd stops because memcache issues a token for a given key at most once every 10 seconds. The first client to miss receives a token and queries the database. Every other client that misses in the next 10 seconds receives no token, getting instead a response telling it to wait 10 ms and read the cache again. The token holder usually writes the value to the cache within a few milliseconds, so the waiting clients' second reads hit the cache. A herd of thousands of database queries becomes one query and a few thousand fast cache reads. If the token holder crashes or fails to set the value, the waiting clients continue to miss until the 10-second lease expires, when the next miss receives a new token. Up to 10 seconds of elevated read latency on a single key is the trade-off for preventing database overload. In the simulation, enabling leases keeps the database load at one query regardless of the read rate. Nishtala and his colleagues report that leases reduced peak database query throughput for hot keys from 17,000 queries a second to 1,300 queries a second.[^peak]

For applications that can tolerate slightly outdated data, memcache provides an optimization. When a key is deleted, the server retains its old value briefly in a recently deleted list, and a waiting client can accept that value, flagged as stale, rather than waiting and retrying. Engineers choose whether to accept stale reads based on the data type: a news feed can display a value that is 1 second old, whereas an account privacy setting cannot.

Engineers can mitigate thundering herds at other layers of the system. A single web server can deduplicate concurrent misses for the same key so that it sends only one database query and makes its other local threads wait for that response. This technique, called **request coalescing**, reduces a herd across 1,000 web servers to at most one query per web server, which still produces 1,000 concurrent database queries if all 1,000 servers miss at once. Alternatively, a client can recompute a cached value slightly before its TTL expires, using a randomized threshold for each read so that one early reader updates the key before the remaining readers experience a miss.[^early] Unlike single-server coalescing, a cache lease coordinates requests across all clients because the cache server itself controls which client queries the database.

In lesson 5, we saw why a client that updates the database deletes the cached key instead of updating the cache directly: if two writers update the cache concurrently, their requests can reach the cache in the opposite order from the database commits, leaving the older value in the cache. Deleting the key avoids write-write races and is idempotent, since deleting an already missing key has no effect. However, deleting on write still leaves a race condition between a reader and a writer. The Facebook paper calls this a **stale set**, which occurs when a slow reader writes an outdated value into the cache after a concurrent update.

In the figure, reader A misses on a key, receives lease token 7, reads the old value v1 from the database, and then pauses (for example, due to a garbage collection pause or network delay). Writer B then commits the new value v2 to the database and deletes the key from the cache. Finally, reader A resumes and attempts to set v1 in the cache.

blocks.caption: A stale set: a slow reader writes an outdated value to the cache after a writer has deleted the key.
blocks.task: Play it with leases off, then with leases on

blocks.text: Without leases, this race leaves the cache permanently out of sync with the database until the next write or TTL expiry. Because writer B has already sent its delete, the cache retains v1, which for an infrequently updated key can last for days. Leases prevent stale sets using the same token mechanism. When writer B deletes the key, memcache invalidates any active lease token for that key. When reader A subsequently sends its set request with token 7, memcache sees that the token has been invalidated, recognises that A's value may predate the delete, and rejects the write. The next reader misses, receives a new token, and fetches v2 from the database.

Leases do not provide strict consistency. In the few milliseconds between writer B committing to the database and deleting the cache key, concurrent readers still read v1 from the cache. Leases instead guarantee bounded staleness: once the cache processes the delete, no reader holding a value read before that delete can write it back into the cache.

Up to this point, the web server that updated the database also sent the delete request to memcache. This client-driven invalidation fails in two scenarios. First, if a web server crashes after committing its database transaction but before sending the cache delete, the stale value remains in the cache indefinitely. Second, Facebook operated multiple **front-end clusters** in each region, each with its own independent pool of memcache servers caching the same database keys. A database write must invalidate the key across every front-end cluster that caches it, and an individual web server does not track which clusters hold copies of a given key.

Facebook solved this by generating cache deletes directly from the database's [[commit log|write]], which records every committed transaction. We saw this log in lesson 4 as the replication stream sent to read replicas. A MySQL primary records each committed change, in commit order, to its binary log. When a web server executed an SQL write transaction, it appended the names of the affected cache keys as comments in the SQL statement, causing MySQL to write those key names into the binary log alongside the data changes. A daemon called **mcsqueal**, running on each database server, tailed the binary log, extracted the cache keys, grouped them into batches, and forwarded the delete requests through a layer of routing proxies to every memcache cluster in the region.

Log-tailing invalidation provides stronger delivery guarantees than client-sent deletes. Because the daemon reads the commit log, it sends deletes only for transactions that actually committed, and it delivers those deletes even if the originating web server crashes immediately after committing. If the mcsqueal daemon itself crashes, it resumes reading from its last saved offset in the log upon restart, ensuring no deletes are dropped. Because each delete invalidates any active lease token on that key, slow readers in any cluster are blocked from completing stale sets. The trade-off is a slightly longer invalidation latency due to log reading and batching. Batching also reduced packet rates across the datacentre network: mcsqueal packed deletes for many keys into a single network packet sent to one router per cluster, whereas individual web servers sending point-to-point deletes would have generated millions of small packets a second. Driving secondary updates from a storage engine's commit log is a standard systems pattern for maintaining caches, search indexes and read replicas, and in lesson 16 we will design an architecture around it.

Nishtala and his colleagues introduced one more mechanism to handle cache misses caused by a memcache server hardware failure. Under standard consistent hashing (lesson 5), removing a failed server from the hash ring reassigns all of its keys to its immediate neighbours on the ring. If the failed server held hot keys, that sudden shift in read load can overload a neighbouring cache server, causing a cascading failure around the ring. To prevent this, Facebook reserved a small pool of idle memcache servers, roughly 1% of the cluster's capacity, called the **gutter**. When a client request to a primary memcache server times out, the client retries the read against the gutter pool, and on a gutter miss, queries the database and writes the value into the gutter. Each key from the failed server misses once in the gutter and is then served from the gutter pool, shielding both the database and the neighbouring cache servers during the outage. Gutter entries use a short, fixed TTL of a few seconds instead of receiving explicit delete requests, trading brief staleness for keeping invalidation traffic off the gutter pool.[^udp]

Facebook served user traffic from datacentres in multiple geographic **regions**. One region was designated the primary and housed the primary MySQL databases, which processed all write transactions. The other regions housed read-only MySQL replicas updated via asynchronous replication, and web servers in those regions read from their local caches and local database replicas. As we saw in lesson 4, asynchronous replication across thousands of kilometres introduces replication lag: a write committed on the US East Coast can take 1 second or more to replicate to a datacentre in Europe.

When asynchronous replication lag interacts with a local cache, a user can observe their own write disappear. The interactive figure models this scenario with two toggles, "Deletes from the commit log" and "Remote marker". Run the simulation with both toggles off first.

blocks.caption: A user in a replica region saves a change and reads it back. Times are illustrative; replication lag across an ocean is often 1 second or more.
blocks.task: Turn on both fixes and play it to the end

blocks.text: Two things go wrong, one after the other. First, the user's own read misses the cache and reads the local replica, which has not yet applied the write, so they see their change undone. Second, that read puts the old value back in the cache, where everyone keeps reading it after the replica has caught up. Taking deletes from the commit log fixes the second: the European replica's own daemon sends the delete after the replica has applied the write, so no copy older than the replica's data can outlive it. It does nothing for the user's first read, which happens before the replica has caught up.

For that, Facebook used a **remote marker**. Before the write, the web server sets a marker key for k in its region's cache, and the marker is removed when the replicated write arrives. A reader that misses on k and finds the marker reads from the primary region instead of the local replica. That read is slower, a round trip across the ocean of perhaps 100 ms, but it happens only for keys written in the last moment, and it gives the person who made the change their own change back. Lesson 4 called this property reading your own writes; lesson 13 placed it among the consistency models. Facebook chose it for writers and left everyone else with eventual consistency, a trade made openly: the paper says it accepts stale reads for most data in return for serving from local replicas.

Running look-aside memcache in front of MySQL had architectural limits for graph queries. In 2013 Facebook also published the design of TAO, a read-through and write-through caching layer purpose-built for its social graph of objects and associations. Because clients send all reads and writes through TAO rather than coordinating cache and database requests themselves, TAO eliminates client-driven cache races by construction.[^tao]

blocks.caption: Six questions on herds, leases and invalidation
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A key is read 20,000 times a second. Its refill query takes 50 ms on an idle database, which can serve about 2,000 such queries a second. Why can its expiry keep it missing for many seconds?
choices: Every miss queries the database, and the duplicate queries slow down the first query whose response would refill the key
Memcache refuses to store a key while other clients are still reading it, so the refill waits for a quiet moment
The cache evicts the key again as soon as it is set, because thousands of clients are asking for it at once
items.why: In 50 ms a thousand readers miss, generating ten times the throughput the database can serve, and the database shares its CPU capacity among them. The refill query slows down, the miss window lasts longer, and more readers send duplicate queries, creating a feedback loop.

items.ask: How do memcache leases stop a thundering herd on a hot key?
choices: They give every client that misses a token, and the database answers token holders in the order they arrived
They hand out a token for a key at most once every 10 seconds, and clients without one wait and read the cache again
They make the cache keep a hot key for ever, so that it never expires and never needs to be refilled
items.why: Only the token holder queries the database. The remaining clients are instructed to wait a few milliseconds, by which time the holder has usually populated the cache, so their retry read is a cache hit.

items.ask: Reader A misses, reads v1 from the database, and stalls. Writer B commits v2 and deletes the key. A then sets v1. With leases, what happens?
choices: Memcache keeps v1, since A was the first to miss and so holds the oldest and strongest claim to the key
Memcache stores v1 but marks it stale, and the next reader replaces it with v2 straight away
Memcache refuses A's set, because B's delete voided the lease token that A was given on its miss
items.why: A delete invalidates outstanding lease tokens on that key. Because A's value may predate the write, memcache rejects A's set request, and the next reader receives a fresh token and reads v2.

items.ask: Why did Facebook send cache invalidations from a daemon reading the database's commit log rather than from the web servers that made the writes?
choices: The log lists every committed write and outlives a crashed web server, so no delete is lost, and the deletes can be batched
Reading the log is faster than sending a delete from the web server, so stale values are removed sooner than before
Web servers sent deletes over UDP, which loses packets, while the daemon's deletes go over TCP and so always arrive
items.why: A web server can crash between committing its transaction and sending its cache delete, and it does not track every memcache cluster that holds the key. The database commit log records every committed write in order and can be re-read from the last checkpoint after a daemon crash. Deletes sent via the log arrive slightly later, not sooner.

items.ask: What problem does a small gutter pool of spare memcache servers solve?
choices: It holds the cache's least-used keys so that the main servers have more memory free for the hot ones
It takes the load of a failed memcache server, so its keys neither hit the database nor overload a neighbour
It stores the recently deleted values that leases hand to waiting clients as stale but acceptable answers
items.why: Rehashing a failed server's keys onto its consistent-hashing neighbours can shift hot keys onto a server that then fails from overload as well. The gutter pool, comprising about 1% of the cluster's servers, absorbs those misses and uses a short TTL instead of explicit invalidation.

items.ask: In a region that reads from a lagging replica, a user saves a change and reloads the page straight away. Which design shows them their change?
choices: Deleting the key from the local cache as soon as the write commits in the primary region, before the reply is sent
Taking deletes from the local replica's commit log, so the cache is cleared once the replica has the write
A remote marker set before the write, so misses on that key read from the primary until the replica catches up
items.why: The first two options clear the cache, but the user's subsequent cache miss still queries the local replica before the replicated write has arrived. The remote marker directs misses for that specific key to the primary region until replication completes.

items.ask: On 23 September 2010 reverting the bad configuration value did not end Facebook's outage. Why not?
choices: The bad value had already been copied to every replica, and replication could not be stopped while the site was running
Clients treated database errors as invalid values and deleted the key, so the overload kept producing more queries
The engineers could not find which value was bad until the site was turned off and the logs could be read
items.why: The feedback loop had become self-sustaining: database overload caused query errors, errors triggered cache deletes, deletes caused cache misses, and misses generated more database queries. Only stopping incoming traffic broke the cycle.

summary: **A miss on a hot key triggers a thundering herd.** Every reader that misses during the cache refill latency sends a duplicate query, so a 50 ms refill of a key read 20,000 times a second generates 1,000 concurrent database queries.

**A thundering herd can create a feedback loop.** When concurrent duplicate queries exceed the database's capacity, they increase the latency of the query that would refill the cache, stretching the miss window from milliseconds to tens of seconds.

**Retry logic can sustain an outage.** Facebook's 2010 outage was driven by error-handling code that deleted the cached key and re-queried the database whenever a database query failed; only stopping client traffic broke the loop.

**A lease grants one client the right to refill a key.** Memcache issues a lease token per key at most once every 10 seconds, while other missing clients wait a few milliseconds and retry their cache read.
**Leases also prevent stale sets.** Deleting a key invalidates any outstanding lease tokens for it, preventing a slow reader from overwriting newer data with a value read before the delete.

**Generate invalidations from the database commit log.** A daemon tailing the database's binary log sends batched deletes for every committed write, ensuring deletes are delivered even if the web server crashes.

**A gutter pool absorbs misses from failed cache servers.** Allocating about 1% of cache servers as spares keeps a failed server's hot keys from overloading the database or neighbouring cache servers.

**Replication lag combined with caching can violate read-your-writes consistency.** Setting a remote marker in the local cache routes misses to the primary region until the local database replica catches up.

johnson.title: The post
johnson.text: Johnson's post, "More Details on Today's Outage", opens by saying the site had been down or unreachable for many people for about 2.5 hours and ends with an apology. It is one of the earliest public accounts of a feedback loop taking down a large site, and it is short, taking up about a page.

ps.title: The database in the figure
ps.text: Processor sharing is a mathematical simplification. Production databases also queue requests at connection pool limits, time queries out and exhaust memory, which causes throughput to drop even more sharply under overload. The numbers in the simulation illustrate the queueing threshold rather than Facebook's exact hardware limits.

peak.title: Seventeen thousand to thirteen hundred
peak.text: The paper reports this reduction as a measured peak query rate across keys experiencing heavy read and write traffic. The simulation's single-query refill represents the ideal case for a single key; in production, lease tokens expire after 10 seconds, token holders fail, and many distinct keys miss concurrently.

early.title: Refreshing early at random
early.text: In 2015 Andrea Vattani, Flavio Chierichetti and Keegan Lowenstein published an optimal probabilistic early expiration algorithm (XFetch). On each cache hit, the client recomputes the value early with a probability that increases exponentially as the key approaches its TTL expiry and scales with the time required to recompute the value. Most reads return the cached value immediately, and with high probability a single reader refreshes the key shortly before it expires.

udp.title: Gets over UDP
udp.text: Facebook's web servers sent memcache read requests over UDP to avoid TCP connection overhead and treated dropped packets as cache misses. Write and delete requests travelled over TCP through mcrouter, a routing proxy that also broadcasts invalidations across memcache clusters.

tao.title: TAO
tao.text: TAO, described by Nathan Bronson and colleagues at the USENIX Annual Technical Conference in June 2013, stores graph objects (users, posts, locations) and associations (likes, friendships, comments). It is optimised for social graph queries such as fetching the most recent 50 comments on a post, using a two-tier hierarchy of follower and leader caches in front of sharded MySQL databases.
